nodes.label: Transcription software
nodes.one_line: Use Audacity or Transcribe! to slow, loop, and EQ a recording, and produce a transcription whose tricky passages you can defend measure by measure.
know_what: Audacity — the free cross-platform editor that is the field's workhorse, with Change Tempo, Change Speed, EQ filters, and a spectrogram view for transcription
Transcribe! (Seventh String) — the commercial slow-down tool built for transcription, with per-track EQ, automatic note detection, and repeatable loop regions
pitch-preserving slowdown — the DSP feature (Audacity's Change Tempo, or WSOLA) that slows audio without the chipmunk transposition, letting you work at 40-75% speed and still hear the real pitches
the loop region — a 3-5 second A-B selection replayed continuously, the standard working unit because the ear cannot hold a longer stretch accurately
band EQ — high-passing around 80-100 Hz to kill room rumble and low-passing or notching to expose a buried line under an interfering instrument
the spectrogram view — Audacity's spectral display of partials and formants, the tie-breaker when two hearings of a pitch conflict
the workflow rule — the software is a prosthetic ear, not a judge: it does not decide pitches, it makes your decisions checkable
know_how: Set the speed to 50% with pitch preservation before notating, and re-verify every written note at full speed afterward
Mark loop regions on the tricky passages — 3-5 seconds each — and replay them until the figure is fully written, before moving on
Apply band EQ to isolate the instrument you transcribe: high-pass at 80-100 Hz against rumble, notch or low-pass against an interfering voice or drone
Switch to the spectrogram view when hearings conflict and read the partials to settle the pitch instead of guessing
Work in speed layers: 75% for the phrase and meter skeleton, 50% for details, 40% or below for ornaments, checking each layer against full speed
Keep the project organized in named tracks — original, slowed, EQ'd — so every reading in the final score is reproducible from the session
Export the transcribed region and do a final full-speed check of the whole passage before captioning the score
habits: Set up the slow/loop/EQ workspace before listening, so the listening time goes to the music, not the menu
Always confirm the final reading at full speed — a slowed loop can manufacture artifacts, like a vibrato heard as two distinct pitches
Keep loops short — 3-5 seconds — because a longer loop blurs the ear's target
When a pitch is uncertain, check the spectrogram before writing it, and note the confirmation
Record the speed and filter settings in the score's caption so the reading is checkable
nodes.checkpoint: Transcribe a 60-second passage you have never heard using Audacity or Transcribe!: work at 40-75% speed with pitch preservation, loop 3-5 second regions, use EQ or the spectrogram to resolve at least two ambiguous passages, and produce a score you can defend measure by measure at full speed.
nodes.common_failure: Using the slow-down as a crutch for the whole file instead of targeted loops, or slowing with Change Speed instead of Change Tempo so the pitch drops and the music becomes unrecognizable — every decision is then made against a distorted artifact and the final score fails a full-speed check.
sources: Audacity manual (audacityteam.org), Change Tempo and spectrogram documentation
Seventh String Transcribe! documentation
Ter Ellingson, 'Transcription' in Ethnomusicology: An Introduction (Myers ed., 1992)

nodes.label: Limits of notation
nodes.one_line: State what your notation cannot show — timbre, microtiming, performance nuance — using Seeger's prescriptive/descriptive distinction, and choose a notation that fits your analytical claim.
know_what: Seeger's prescriptive/descriptive distinction (1958) — prescriptive notation tells a performer what to do, descriptive records what was heard, and no single notation does both
timbre — the sound quality (a kora's attack, a throat singer's overtones) that staff notation cannot encode, recoverable only by listening or spectrogram
microtiming — sub-beat deviations, down to tens of milliseconds (a percussionist behind the beat, a singer's rubato), that note values and barlines average away
performance nuance — ornamentation, portamento, breath, dynamic shaping, the layer conventionally dropped as 'expression'
the analytical claim as notation driver — the notation choice follows the claim: pitch structure calls for staff, timing calls for a timeline or graphical rendering
graphical notation — waveform and spectrogram renderings (Sonic Visualiser, Praat) that show what the staff drops, at the cost of easy reading
the map-territory error — treating the score as the music; a transcription is an analysis artifact, and its caption must say what it omits
know_how: Before notating, list what your claim needs — pitch, timing, timbre — and choose the notation that actually carries it
Write the caption naming the notation system, labeling it prescriptive or descriptive in Seeger's terms, and listing the features deliberately omitted
When a feature defeats staff notation, switch notation for that feature — a timeline row for timing, a spectrogram for timbre — rather than forcing it onto the staff
Report microtiming deviations in milliseconds or cents where they carry meaning, instead of rounding them into the grid
Re-listen to the recording against the completed score and mark every place the score simplifies, so the reader can hear the difference
State the claim the notation serves, so the reader can judge whether the omissions matter for it
habits: Ask before choosing: what does this notation claim to show, and what does it silently drop?
Treat a suspiciously clean score as a warning sign, not an achievement
Keep a margin layer for what the notation cannot carry, so no information is silently discarded
When asked what the piece sounds like, reach for the recording, not the score
Keep the measured and the approximated distinct in the notes, and say which is which in the caption
nodes.checkpoint: Given a 30-second passage that defeats staff notation — microtiming, timbre, or nuance — write a one-page caption: name the notation chosen, label it prescriptive or descriptive in Seeger's terms, list the features deliberately omitted, and cite the analytical claim the choice serves.
nodes.common_failure: Reaching for staff notation by default and letting the clean score stand for the music: microtiming averaged into the grid, timbre dropped as 'expression,' and the analysis then done on the score rather than the sound — the map is mistaken for the territory.
sources: Charles Seeger, 'Prescriptive and Descriptive Music-Writing' (1958)
Ter Ellingson, 'Transcription' in Ethnomusicology: An Introduction (Myers ed., 1992)
Bruno Nettl, The Study of Ethnomusicology (2005), chapter on transcription

nodes.label: Scale & mode analysis
nodes.one_line: Classify a piece's scale or mode system — raga, maqam, sléndro/pélog, pentatonic set — from measured intervals, and name the system the tradition itself uses.
know_what: raga — the North Indian melodic system in which the scale (thaat) is only a frame; identity lives in phrase grammar (pakad), the primary note (vadi), ornamentation, and mood
maqam — the Arab modal system built from tetrachords (ajnas), with microtonal intervals and melodic development rules; the octave scale alone does not define it

sléndro and pélog — the Javanese/Balinese tuning systems: 5-tone sléndro with near-equal steps of roughly 240 cents, and 7-tone pélog with unequal steps, both played in subsets that must be measured, not assumed
the pentatonic set — the five-note collection (e.g., anhemitonic C-D-E-G-A) that recurs worldwide; classifying it as 'pentatonic' is the start of analysis, not the conclusion
the cent — 100 cents per equal-tempered semitone, the field's lingua franca for reporting tunings the staff cannot show (Ellis's 1885 system)
interval measurement — extracting fundamental frequency from sustained tones in Praat or Sonic Visualiser and converting the ratios to cents
the tradition's own name — the emic category (this is raga Bhairavi, this is maqam Rast) that the analyst must match before importing analyst categories
the mode as behavior — a mode is a set of moves, not a set of notes: which degrees are stressed, which are avoided, how phrases begin and end
know_how: Extract the pitch collection first: measure the fundamental frequency of each scale degree on a sustained note in Praat or Sonic Visualiser and convert to cents
Report the measured cents against equal temperament — e.g., sléndro degrees near 0, 230, 480, 700, 960 cents — instead of rounding to staff positions
Match the measured collection against the tradition's own scale names before applying any imported category

Identify the mode by its defining behavior beyond the scale: for raga, the pakad and vadi; for maqam, the jins chain and starting tone; for a pentatonic set, the interval pattern (anhemitonic vs hemitonic)
State the tuning basis in the analysis caption — measured cents or assumed equal temperament — so the reader can judge the classification
Take two independent measurements of each degree and report the spread, discarding measurements taken during obvious ornamentation
Account for the instrument's fixed tuning (a gamelan's sléndro is a property of the instrument) before judging any single performance 'out of tune'
habits: Measure first, name second: read the cents before applying any scale label
When a scale 'looks like' a familiar one, verify it against the tradition's own names before writing it down
Report tuning deviations in cents rather than rounding into the tempered grid
Remember the mode is a behavior, not a collection: ask what the tradition does with the scale
Note the instrument and its tuning constraints alongside every measurement
nodes.checkpoint: Given a recording, measure the pitch collection of a scale passage in cents with two independent measurements per degree, classify it against the tradition's own system — raga, maqam, sléndro/pélog, or pentatonic variant — and write a caption stating the tuning basis and the deviations from equal temperament.
nodes.common_failure: Classifying by ear and rounding into a familiar scale: labeling a sléndro as 'pentatonic' or a maqam as 'a minor scale with a quarter-tone,' skipping the cent measurement — the imported category then carries Western assumptions the tradition does not share, and the analysis is wrong at the foundation.
sources: Nazir Jairazbhoy, The Rāgs of North Indian Music (1971)
Habib Hassan Touma, The Music of the Arabs (1996)
Jaap Kunst, Music in Java (1949)
Alexander Ellis, 'On the Musical Scales of Various Nations' (1885)

nodes.label: Rhythmic analysis
nodes.one_line: Describe a piece's rhythmic structure — metrical framework, timeline, polyrhythm, improvisatory variation — in terms the musicians would recognize.
know_what: the metrical framework — the isochronous pulse grid (e.g., 4/4) Western notation assumes; many traditions do not organize time that way
the timeline — the repeating reference pattern (the West African bell pattern, the Afro-Cuban clave) that an ensemble orients to, often not on the 'downbeat' Western meter expects
additive meter — rhythm built from unequal groupings (aksak: 7/8 as 2+2+3 or 3+2+2) that barlines can carry only if the grouping is set right
tala — the Indian rhythmic cycle (tintal 16 beats as 4+4+4+4, jhaptal 10 as 2+3+2+3) organized as a repeating cycle with claps and waves, not a measure
polyrhythm — simultaneous conflicting layers at different beat ratios (3 against 2, 12 against 16) that a single staff stacks awkwardly
the tuplet — the notational patch (triplets, quintuplets) used to force non-isochronous or cross rhythms onto the metrical grid
improvisatory variation — rhythm as variation on a template where the grid is background, not law (jazz, maqam, and much ritual music)
the emic rhythmic category — the musicians' own name and account of the pattern (clave, timeline, tala name) that the analysis must preserve
know_how: Find the timeline first: tap the repeating reference pattern — bell, clave, drum cycle — before describing any single part
Identify the cycle and its internal grouping: for tala, count the beats and the subdivisions (tintal 4+4+4+4, jhaptal 2+3+2+3), naming the cycle if it has one
Set barlines to the actual groupings for additive meters (2+2+3, 3+3+2) instead of forcing the passage into 4/4
Map the polyrhythm by the beat ratio between layers (3:2, 12:16) and notate each layer against the timeline rather than against a single downbeat
Separate the musicians' own rhythmic categories from analyst categories, and label each claim accordingly
Choose the notation from the structure: metrical staff for isochronous music, a timeline-plus-parts diagram for cycle-based music
Check the reading with a musician who knows the tradition: can they reproduce the structure you drew, and do they recognize it in their own terms?
habits: Never draw barlines before you can tap the timeline
When a rhythm 'won't fit,' suspect the grid, not the music
Name the pattern in the tradition's terms when it has one — clave, timeline, tala name
Keep the timeline visible in the analysis, since the parts relate to it
Test the notation by clapping it back: if a performer cannot reproduce your rhythm from the score, the notation is wrong

know_why.claim: Western metrical notation can represent non-Western rhythm adequately: additive and cycle-based meters are notatable if barlines follow the real groupings and tuplets and timeline diagrams carry the rest.
know_why.because: Notation is a tool, not a theory: with correctly grouped barlines, tuplets, and a supplementary timeline, a competent reader can reconstruct an aksak 7/8 or a 16-beat tala well enough to analyze and compare it — and giving up notation for rhythm would forfeit the comparability the field's analyses depend on.
know_why.disputed_by: Kofi Agawu and the critics of 'structural listening' hold that Western notation is not a neutral grid but a theory: it hears meter where other traditions hear timelines, hierarchy where they hear cycles, and the tuplets that 'patch' the grid still force the music through a Western lens, systematically misrepresenting what is actually played.
know_why.source: Kofi Agawu, 'Structural Analysis or Cultural Analysis? Competing Perspectives on the "Standard Pattern" of West African Rhythm' (Journal of the American Musicological Society 59/1, 2006); Simha Arom, African Polyphony and Polyrhythm (1991); Martin Clayton, Time in Indian Music (2000)

nodes.checkpoint: Given a recording with non-isochronous or cycle-based rhythm, produce an analysis that names the timeline or tala with its internal grouping, maps the layers' beat ratios, and sets notation to the actual groupings — then have a musician who knows the tradition confirm the structure in their own terms.
nodes.common_failure: Imposing 4/4 and tuplet-patching the discrepancies: an aksak 7/8 becomes '4/4 with a funny accent,' the timeline is read as an off-beat error, and the analysis describes a grid the musicians never played — the emic structure is lost entirely.
sources: Kofi Agawu, Representing African Music (2003)
Simha Arom, African Polyphony and Polyrhythm (1991)
Martin Clayton, Time in Indian Music (2000)
Konstantin Brăiloiu, 'Le rythme aksak' (1951)

nodes.label: Cultural interpretation
nodes.one_line: Interpret a musical feature — a mode, a drum pattern, a song text — as cultural meaning (function, identity, emotion) in the tradition's own terms, following Merriam's 'music in culture'.
know_what: 'music in culture' — Merriam's frame (The Anthropology of Music, 1964): music is part of culture and its meanings are assigned by social context
'music as culture' — Feld's reframing: music does not just sit in culture but constitutes it; sound structures social life (Sound and Sentiment, 1982)
Merriam's tripartite model — conceptualization (beliefs about music), behavior (who performs, when, how), and sound; a full interpretation connects all three
Merriam's functions — what music does: emotional expression, aesthetic enjoyment, entertainment, communication, symbolic representation, and the rest of the ten
function vs meaning — what music accomplishes versus what it says; the two are often conflated and must be kept distinct in the write-up
emic interpretation — meaning in the tradition's own terms, grounded in consultants' accounts rather than the analyst's associations
the consultants' voice — the primary evidence for meaning; every meaning claim should be attributable to a consultant, an observation, or a text
thick description — Geertz's method (1973) of reading meaning from action and context, the interpretive school's working procedure
sound as social structure — Feld's Kaluli analysis: bird calls, weeping, and song linked in a single system of meaning, the model for this kind of interpretation
know_how: Take one musical feature — a mode, a drum pattern, a song text — and ask first what it does in its context, then what it says
Collect consultants' accounts of the feature's meaning before offering your own, and attribute every meaning claim to its source
Connect the three layers of Merriam's model: the belief about the music, the behavior around it, and the sound itself
Write the interpretation with evidence: quote the consultant, cite the recorded passage, name the occasion and setting
Check the reading against the emic account — would the tradition recognize the meaning you propose? If not, revise or label it as your own reading
Keep function and meaning in separate labeled columns in the draft, weaving them only when both are solid
Re-listen to the recording with the proposed meaning in view, and test whether the sound actually supports it
habits: Ask consultants what the music means before deciding yourself
Treat a meaning claim without a consultant, observation, or text behind it as a hypothesis, not a finding
Keep the sound in view: interpretation that ignores the music is anthropology, not ethnomusicology
Run each interpretation through Merriam's triad — belief, behavior, sound — and check that all three are connected
Re-listen to the recording after forming the interpretation: does the sound make sense in those terms?

know_why.claim: Musical meaning is assigned by context — music 'in culture,' in Merriam's phrase: a drum pattern or mode carries the meaning its society gives it, so interpretation must start from the social context, not the sound alone.
know_why.because: The same sound means different things in different societies — a drum rhythm can be a work signal, a funeral lament, or a courtship call — so the analyst who reads meaning off the sound alone imports their own culture's associations; grounding interpretation in context is what makes it accountable to the tradition.
know_why.disputed_by: Steven Feld and the 'music as culture' camp hold that music is not a passive carrier of externally assigned meanings but itself constitutes social life — sound structures feeling and society, as in his Kaluli analysis — so treating music as merely 'in' culture misses the cultural work the music itself is doing.
know_why.source: Alan P. Merriam, The Anthropology of Music (1964); Steven Feld, Sound and Sentiment: Birds, Weeping, Poetics, and Song in Kaluli Expression (1982)

nodes.checkpoint: Given a musical feature from your fieldwork or a recording, write a 500-word interpretation: the function, the meaning in consultants' own terms quoted and attributed, the belief and behavior layers connected to the sound, with every claim traceable to a consultant, observation, or recorded passage.
nodes.common_failure: Interpreting from the analyst's own musical associations: a drum pattern 'feels sad' to you, so it is a lament — with no consultant evidence, no context, and no connection to the tradition's own categories — the reading says more about the analyst's culture than about the music.
sources: Alan P. Merriam, The Anthropology of Music (1964)
Steven Feld, Sound and Sentiment (1982)
Clifford Geertz, The Interpretation of Cultures (1973)

nodes.label: Cross-cultural comparison
nodes.one_line: Compare two traditions on a single dimension — melody, rhythm, function — with a controlled method like Lomax's cantometrics or a parameter you define, while acknowledging what the comparison flattens.
know_what: controlled comparison — comparing two traditions on one defined dimension with explicit criteria, so the result is checkable rather than impressionistic
cantometrics — Lomax's coding system (Folk Song Style and Culture, 1968): roughly 3,000 songs coded on 37 scales — vocal timbre, phrasing, orchestral texture — to map singing styles worldwide
the coding scheme — a fixed rubric with named categories and anchors (e.g., a 1-5 scale for melodic range defined by interval examples) applied by raters to every sample item
the dimension — the single feature compared (melody, rhythm, function); comparing two things at once usually means neither is done carefully
the sample — the defined set of performances coded; a comparison's scope is bounded by its sample, and a claim about 'African rhythm' is really a claim about the sample behind it
inter-rater reliability — the check that two coders score the same item the same way; disagreement exposes vague categories
the flattening — what comparison necessarily drops: context, meaning, emic categories, and individual creativity, all of which a coding scale averages away
repertory vs performance — comparing what is played (repertory) and how it is played (performance) are different projects with different evidence
know_how: Define the dimension and the sample before coding: what is compared, how many performances from each tradition, from what sources
Build the coding scheme with explicit categories and anchors — every scale value defined by an example a second coder can apply
Apply the scheme to both traditions' samples, coding blind to your hypothesis where possible to avoid biasing the ratings
Report inter-rater reliability when more than one coder is involved, and fix the categories it exposes as vague
State in the write-up what the comparison flattens — context, meaning, emic categories, individual variation — and why the dimension still earns its comparison
Compare the same dimension with the same instrument: two things given the same name are not the same thing unless the coding says so
Bound the conclusion by the sample: say which corpus the finding is about, and refuse to extend it beyond the coded performances
habits: Before comparing, write down what the comparison will flatten — and keep that list visible in the analysis
Ask whose categories the comparison uses; if they are the analyst's, say so
Pilot the coding scheme on a few items before the full run, and revise the categories that collapse under use
Treat a cross-cultural 'similarity' as a hypothesis about both traditions, checked in each, not a free-standing fact
When a comparison claims something big, ask which sample it is actually about before accepting it

know_why.claim: Controlled comparison is the scientific core of ethnomusicology: coding performances on defined scales — as Lomax's cantometrics did for roughly 3,000 songs across more than 200 cultures — lets claims about musical style be tested across traditions instead of asserted impressionistically.
know_why.because: A single tradition's analysis cannot answer distributional questions — where a style occurs, what correlates with it — and only a systematic, replicable coding scheme applied to a defined sample yields results another researcher can check, which is what separates comparative claims from travel writing.
know_why.disputed_by: the interpretive school, which calls cantometrics reductionist and decontextualizing: a performance's coded 'vocal rasp' or 'texture' strips away meaning, emic categories, and local context, so the comparison compares fragments and mistakes its own coding categories for musical reality — Feld's critique of Lomax's linguistic model is the canonical statement.
know_why.source: Alan Lomax, Folk Song Style and Culture (1968); Steven Feld, 'Linguistic Models in Ethnomusicology' (Ethnomusicology 18/2, 1974); Bruno Nettl, The Study of Ethnomusicology (2005), comparative chapters

nodes.checkpoint: Compare two traditions on one defined dimension: build a coding scheme with explicit anchors, code a defined sample of at least five performances from each tradition, report the results with the scheme attached so a colleague could replicate the coding, and write up both the finding and what the comparison flattens.
nodes.common_failure: Comparing with no defined scheme: 'African drumming is more rhythmic than Western' — a conclusion with no coded dimension, no sample, and no acknowledgment of what is dropped, which a single counter-example destroys and which hands the interpretive school its case.
sources: Alan Lomax, Folk Song Style and Culture (1968)
Steven Feld, 'Linguistic Models in Ethnomusicology' (Ethnomusicology 18/2, 1974)
Bruno Nettl, The Study of Ethnomusicology (2005), comparative chapters
